item.title: How we save entry-level UX work that teaches craft in the time of AI. Our field depends on this.
item.description: The craft was learned at this table, one marked-up screen at a time. AI assisted,Automation is taking tasks juniors learned on. Here are seven tasks that put the practice back so we keep human element of user experience and build the bench for 2030.Many teams I know have stopped assigning transcript tagging because now AI does it. Their platform of choice returns sessions tagged, themed, and clipped transcripts before anyone opens them, and does it well enough.Nobody argued, and nobody wrote down what else that task did.Tagging transcripts is how researchers and designers learn that people say “it’s fine” when they mean they gave up, which AI never picks up. Marking redlines is how a new designer learns which spacing decisions the system made and which are open.That work was never worth much as output; it taught the skills needed to repeat in the future so they learned the craft. It was worth a great deal as practice, and the two arrived bundled: cheap judgments under supervision, where being wrong cost nothing.The numbers of this change are already in.Source: Canaries in the Coal MineErik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, working from payroll records through June 2026 in Canaries in the Coal Mine, find employment for 22 to 25 year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations sitting 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, and no comparable gap for experienced workers.The adjustment runs through hiring, not layoffs. And that’s risk that our field doesn’t have the skills to move forward in the future as more than a competency.Their proposed mechanism is the part design leaders should sit with: AI substitutes for codified knowledge and complements the tacit kind, built by doing, and a lot of designers aren’t doing a lot of doing right now.I cared about building for that future that I mentored designers continuously during the 2010’s, spoke at University of Washingston and taught part-time as part of General Assembly.I know, I know, but at least my previous students are doing well.This is an important moment for all of us and we need to take action. Here are seven moves we can do to put the put the practice back and save the field for the design and research generations to come.A photo of when I was teaching a class at Generel Assembly.Inventory the tasks automation removedStart with an inventory, and keep it boring. List every task that left the junior queue in the last 18 months, some of which I actually wrote a book about, uxGPT.On most teams the list looks like this:Transcript tagging and synthesis. Sessions come back tagged, themed, and clipped before anyone opens the recording.First-pass wireframes. A prompt returns four layouts in the time it took a junior to sketch one.Screener drafts. Recruiting tools generate screening questions straight from a study goal.Competitive audits. A model walks the competitor’s flow and summarizes the patterns.Redline sheets. Design tools export spacing, type, and token values without a handoff document.Meeting notes and status summaries. Written and posted before the call ends.Inventory ExampleThen add a second column: what did that task teach the person doing it? A competitive audit is worthless as a deliverable. Building one is how a designer learns that competitors solved onboarding five ways, and that four of them are bad for reasons you only see up close.Future of User Research Report 2026Maze’s Future of User Research Report 2026 found 69% of research professionals now use AI in at least some projects, up 19 points in a year, concentrated in transcription, synthesis, and drafting questions — where a junior used to start.Ethan Mollick makes the case for doing this on purpose in Choosing to Stay Human: the defaults for what work gets handed to AI are being set right now, mostly without planning, and they will be hard to reverse once a generation of workers has built habits around them. The inventory is how you set yours deliberately.Run it with your seniors in the room.They can tell you the screener draft was where they learned to write a question that doesn’t leak the answer. Without those stories you have a list of chores, and you will conclude that nothing was lost.A task can be worthless as output and foundational as training.That pairing is the bundle: a lesson riding along inside work somebody had to do anyway, invoiced to nobody.Look hardest at those, because the business case for automating them is airtight and the training case never got written down.The junior makes the call. The senior asks why and uses it as a teaching moment.Assign juniors real decisions with guardrailsSurgery ran this experiment first for a pretty long time.Matt Beane spent two years watching robotic and open operations for Shadow Learning: Building Robotic Surgical Skill When Approved Means Fail. Open surgery needed the resident’s hands; on the robot, the attending works alone while the resident watches a screen.Sometimes the robot does the skills the surgeon should be doing.A national survey of recent United States general surgery graduates, published in 2025, found only 37% reported high autonomy in robotic cases, against 89% in open ones. Same programs, different console.The analogy has a limit, since design has no credentialing gate. The mechanism is what transfers: when the expert can finish without the novice’s hands, the novice stops learning.The senior prompts, evaluates, and revises while the junior watches the screen and takes the notes.Everyone is busy. One person is learning.So give them the call: which direction goes to the review, which participants come out of the recruit. Julie Zhuo’s The Looking Glass reduces design levels to a line: the more senior the designer, the more abstract the problem.Pick reversible calls — I call them two way doors, which is a mental model Jeff Bezos has— and let them stand.Beane’s The Skill Code names challenge as the missing ingredient, and challenge means being able to get it wrong, safely.The junior runs the session. The senior takes the notes.Give juniors real work where mistakes are cheapResearchers already drew this line. User Interviews surveyed 150 researchers in May 2026 for its State of Synthetic Users report: nearly all use AI somewhere, and only 8% regularly use synthetic participants. The field automated everything around the conversation and kept the conversation.Synthetic users — not quite ready for prime time, according to most researchers.Keep juniors on the near side. A live session is the one rep with no substitute, and the one most quietly reassigned. Teresa Torres argues the team building the product should interview a customer every week, and that the habit only holds when booked.One session a month with the junior moderating costs a fumbled follow-up, not the recruit, and do it without AI other than the transcription.Between sessions, juniors need work where being wrong is survivable: internal tools, admin screens, the settings page, bulk actions the operations team will complain about at length. The reflex is to point a tool at them, the most automatable work you have.That is your training ground, and once it is gone you are asking people to learn on the checkout flow.Jared M. Spool built Center Centre, a design school, around the same principle. In Interview: Jared Spool on Center Centre, Real Projects, and the Future of UX Education, he describes hiring managers’ near-universal complaint that graduates were not ready to do the work, and a curriculum built on real client projects in response.With this approach that’s been around for centuries, the Labor Department reports 91% of registered apprentices retain employment after their programs end, on the strength of graduated responsibility on real work.Find the two claims the AI transcripts don’t support.Make verification of AI output the deliverableMicrosoft Research and Carnegie Mellon surveyed 319 knowledge workers about 936 real tasks for The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking, presented at CHI 2025.Two findings run in opposite directions.Higher confidence in the tool predicts less critical thinking.Higher confidence in your own ability predicts more.A junior has the least self-confidence on the team and the most exposure to polished machine output, the worst possible combination. Left alone they defer, and deference looks like competence right up until the day it doesn’t.Automation bias is a thing, and a junior has to learn to mitigiate that.This is automation bias, an entry I maintain over at UX Guidelines, arriving early in a career instead of late.Dan Maccarone rebuilt his studio’s process around these tools and came back with a warning that has nothing to do with speed. In Never mind the prompts, here’s the thinking, he names the failure mode: high-speed mediocrity, work that shows up faster precisely because nobody slowed down to think.His sprints stayed five days long and what changed was how much reasoning the deliverables carried, and that is the part a junior is least equipped to notice is missing.To do this, make the critique the thing they hand in.Not “summarize these eight interviews,” but: here is the synthesis the tool produced, find the two claims the transcripts do not support, and bring the timestamps.Real human in the loop with a judgement call.Erika Hall ends Let’s Stop Doing Research with a three-word instruction that could headline the assignment: believe and verify. Her larger point is that inquiry is part of design rather than a phase beside it, which is exactly the habit this exercise is trying to build before anyone thinks of it as research. Grade the catch, not the polish, and say so in the review where the team can hear it.Verification is a skill, and it only builds when somebody (and not some machine) is accountable for the verdict.Do this weekly for a quarter and you have a researcher who reads output with suspicion. Skip it, and you have someone who forwards it.Where we have to get to is this: Higher confidence builds taste and judgement, and that takes practice. A lot of it.Deciding what good looks like, one output at a time.Give juniors the AI evaluation workAI features created a new layer of design work, and nobody has claimed it.Every AI feature needs someone to write the specification the model works from, assemble the cases it is tested against, categorize what it gets wrong, decide what happens when it fails, and set the ship threshold. Right now that happens in fragments, done by whichever senior has an afternoon.Hand it over by giving a junior designer the evaluation set for one feature: 30 real inputs from actual users, the output you would accept for each, and the failures sorted into named categories.Nobody can build that without first deciding what good looks like.That is judgment, written out as a deliverable.OpenAI’s GDPval benchmark has expert graders compare model deliverables against work from professionals averaging 14 years of experience, on tasks that took those experts about seven hours each. The best models were rated as good as or better than the human deliverable in just under half of cases. The other half is the job, and knowing which half you are looking at is a skill somebody has to build.This pairing already has a public example. Josh Clark, with three decades in the field, wrote Sentient Design with Veronika Kindred, a designer much earlier in her career, and in Beyond the Happy Path they describe the gap between their vantage points as the point.She questions practices built for static interfaces.He brings the history of hype cycles.Both halves are needed to judge what an AI feature should do.Two guardrails. It has to carry a decision, so name who says ship or hold, and it has to attach to a feature real users touch.The domain is learned sitting next to the people who do the job. That’s contextual inquiry.Assign each junior a business domainGeneralist screen-making is the most substitutable work in the building. Knowing how the business runs is the least.MIT’s Project NANDA reviewed more than 300 enterprise AI deployments and found 95% of generative AI pilots producing no measurable impact on profit and loss, as Fortune reported in August 2025. The 95% is contested and the report was never peer reviewed, so take the direction rather than the decimal.The direction is the useful part.The researchers blame a learning gap rather than model quality: tools that never adapt to the workflow that were bought to change. Closing it takes somebody who knows that workflow well enough to say what adapting would mean.Make that somebody your junior. Assign a domain, not a component, and have AI equip them with a starting set of questions to remind them this is a business. Their job is to become the person who can explain how a claim gets denied, why the underwriter overrides the recommendation twice a week, and what happens when customs paperwork lands late.None of that is written down, and is hidden in the white space of the job.Nobody automates knowledge that was never written down, it sits with the nine people in operations who do the work.That means standing time with the business, not a research request filed through a manager. Four hours a month with claims adjudicators, and after six months a junior knows the domain better than the senior who spent those months in review meetings.An honest conversation I had with a designer recently — in their environment, designers weren’t being hired back because they didn’t understand their domain enough to make a business impact, while we should have been learning it all along. And then I asked them directly if the designers should be hired back, and he said “No” and he taught UX.We can’t support our own because we haven’t trained them to function in the businesses they work in. This is a way to fix it.One guardrail: Pick a domain with a real owner on the business side who will take the meetings, or you have assigned homework instead of a beat.Put training on the calendar and assign a dollar amount to itEvery move above costs senior time. A junior making the call is slower, and the review takes longer than doing it yourself. Pretending otherwise is how these programs die in month three.So put it in the estimate.Unbundled training is a purchase, and purchases have prices. Start at 10% more senior time on any project with a junior decision owner, a guess rather than a benchmark, then correct it with your own numbers.Mentorship is the first thing cut when a date slips.Peter Merholz, writing in February 2026 that design leaders are failing the next generations, points out that hiring managers prefer senior designers by better than two to one, and that plenty of companies now assume tools will cover the junior tier.He also notes the pattern predates the current tools.AI did not invent this problem — we’ve had it for years, quite honestly— and it removed the last excuse for not fixing it.Notice how quietly it happens. The Stanford decline runs through reduced hiring rather than separations, so no meeting ever decides to stop training the field. A requisition gets written a level higher than last year’s, and again the year after.Conversely, Nielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 describes the other side: junior supply outpacing junior roles, and openings asking for judgment rather than artifacts.Nobody stocks a market for judgment you declined to build.Hire only seniors for a decade and you will bid against every company that made the same call, for a pool nobody grew, including yourself.Training is now a budget lineNone of this requires slowing down the tools, and none of it is nostalgia for busywork. Tagging transcripts by hand was tedious. The tedium was the price of a lesson, and now the lesson needs a different delivery mechanism.What changed is that the training used to be free. It arrived bundled with work somebody had to do anyway, which meant no leader ever had to argue for it, defend it in a planning meeting, or write it into a number. That bundle is gone. Judgment now has to be bought on purpose, in senior hours, on projects with real stakes, or it does not get built at all.The decision in front of every design leader is small and immediate. One field in a template. One inverted session a month. One line in an estimate.None of it shows up in this quarter’s numbers, and all of it shows up in who is qualified to run your practice in 2032.The next generation of judgment comes from the same place it always did: people making real calls, early, while somebody experienced is close enough to catch the fall. The only difference now is that you have to schedule it.Where you can start this weekRun the two-column inventory. List every task that left the junior queue since early 2025, and write what each one taught next to it. An hour of work, and the worry becomes a list.Add a decision owner field to your project template. Every project names one non-senior person accountable for a real call, in writing, before work starts. If the field is empty, the project is not staffed for training.Put training hours in the estimate. Add a line, defend it in planning, and report against it. A cost you can name survives a schedule slip, and one you absorb quietly does not.Those three make the rest possible. The sessions, the domain, and the evaluation set all need somebody accountable and hours nobody has to steal.How we save entry-level UX work that teaches craft in the time of AI. Our field depends on this. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: What the Bible got right about AI
item.description: Michelangelo painted God giving life to man. We are the ones reaching now, and the spark has become a string of code.On making minds, worshipping our own creations, and the ancient warnings we ignored to do exactly what it forbade.The first thing the Bible tells you about human beings is that we wanted to be gods, and it nearly killed us.There is a garden, and in it one forbidden tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A serpent makes the pitch. Eat from it, he tells the woman, and “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”She eats. The man eats. Their eyes open, and humanity never recovers.God’s reaction isn’t rage so much as alarm. The human, God says, “has become like one of us,” and then, worried the creature will reach for the tree of life next and never die, God exiles them from the garden before they can grab it.That story is more relevant today than ever before. The oldest story in the Bible is about a creature reaching for a power meant to belong to its maker, godlike knowledge, the ability to create and to know, and paying for the reach.Humans don’t create from nothing. We rearrange what already exists. We recombine. Only God, in the story, makes something out of the void. The book blesses making. It also warns, again and again, about reaching too far, which is exactly what happened in the garden.It happens again at Babel, where a united humanity builds a tower toward heaven and God looks down and says, in Alter’s translation, that now “nothing they plot to do will be beyond them”, and treats that not as a triumph but as a threat to shut down.Joel S. Baden reads the whole opening of Genesis as one repeating pattern: the story of God “slowly realizing the potential power that his creation might yield if left unchecked,” and restricting it, again and again, as humans reach too far.The Bible never says “don’t build a mind.” It couldn’t have imagined the option. That pattern, human capability outrunning the wisdom to hold it, points straight at us. It also explains why the calls to simply stop, to pause the labs, to slow the whole thing down, keep failing.You are asking a species that reaches, again and again, past what it can safely hold, to not reach for the most powerful thing it has ever imagined. That is the whole reason the industry is hard to regulate, and Genesis saw the problem first. We don’t stop making things because they’re dangerous. We never have.The strange thing is that When we train these models, we are building in the image of us, not God. We are the copy, running the copier. Whatever is in us gets passed down the line.What’s in us is documented. Emily M. Bender and her colleagues argue that these systems absorb our biases and stereotypes and reproduce them at scale.Similarly, Samuel Gehman and his team posit that they generate our cruelty too, sliding into racist and toxic language from prompts that started out innocent, because that language was in the pile we trained them on.We built it out of everything we are, the brilliance and the venom both, and called the result a mind.What comes out is a mirror of humanity, and it inherits all of humanity. The brilliance, the lies, the tenderness, the venom. We keep asking whether AI will turn out good or evil, as if it were a soul with a conscience. The better question is the one Genesis asks on page one. What is actually in the image, and what happens when you make a copy of a creature who is himself a mix of the divine and the fallen?In our own image we made it,after our likeness,and it carried all that we are,the glory and the fall alike.We didn’t make a god. We made a mirror. We are about to find out what we actually look like.The breath in the dustDust it has none, and breath it has none. The thing that cannot die was never alive.We ask whether the machine is conscious and the question is serious enough that the top AI research conference once brought in the philosopher David Chalmers to answer it, because the engineers couldn’t. We are asking the wrong question and the Bible asks a sharper one.Go back to how the first human gets made. Not in the grand cosmic overture of Genesis 1, but in the intimate, hands-in-the-dirt version in Genesis 2. In Alter’s translation, “the Lord God formed the human of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living creature.”Dust, formed. Breath, added. And the result is not “a living soul,” the way the old King James has it, but, in the more careful Hebrew Alter is following, “a living creature.”In Hebrew, nephesh chayyah, are the same two words Genesis already used for the fish and the birds and the beasts. The human isn’t given a soul the animals lack. The human is what the animals are, dust with breath in it.This is the thing the scholarship has been saying for a long time and the culture keeps forgetting. In Hebrew, you do not have a soul. You are a nephesh. John L. McKenzie called it “the concrete existing self.”Hans Walter Wolff, in what is still the standard study of how the Hebrew Bible understands a human being, put it even more plainly, saying nephesh “does not say what a man has, but who the person is.”We are not a ghost riding around in a body or a detachable spirit that survives when the meat gives out.We are, instead, a whole living, breathing, hungry, mortal thing, all at once. Take away the dust and you have no creature. Take away the breath and you have no creature. A nephesh is what happens when the two meet, and it is inseparable from both.An AI has no dust. It has no breath. It has no body to die. What it has is language, an ocean of it, and a staggering ability to arrange that language into shapes that look like the output of a living creature.Emily Bender and Alexander Koller made the sharpest version of the point years before ChatGPT. Imagine, they wrote, a hyper-intelligent octopus that taps into an undersea cable and listens to two people texting. Given enough traffic, the octopus learns to predict and imitate the patterns perfectly, well enough to slip into the conversation and pass as human.It has mastered the form of the language completely. It has no idea what any of it means, because it has never seen a coconut or a rope or a person, never touched the world the words point to.A system trained only on form, they argued, has “a priori no way to learn meaning.”The central claim of Christianity, the one the whole religion balances on, is that the Word became flesh. Language, the Logos, the ordering reason of the universe, took on dust and breath and became a living creature that could bleed and die.The direction only goes one way in the Bible. Word becomes flesh. The abstract becomes the embodied. Meaning takes on a mortal thing to carry it.We are going the other way. We take flesh, the writing and thought and recorded selves of billions of people, every one of them a nephesh with dust and breath, and grind it down into word. Into form without meaning. We are performing the incarnation in reverse and calling the result a mind.The dream underneath that, a mind with no body, floating free of dust and breath, originates from Plato, the separable, immortal soul, the mind as the real thing and the body as its prison. We have quietly resurrected that fantasy and called it the future.Benjamin Blosser sums up the Hebrew side of it: the nephesh is “the totality of conscious, bodily life,” a person you cannot separate from the body that lives it.The newest counterargument agrees. For two million years, every fluent, responsive, human-seeming signal came from a body with what Sheila L. Macrine calls “metabolic stakes,” something that could be hungry, be hurt, and die.The language model is the first thing in history to produce all the signals of a living mind with none of the stakes. Gary Marcus, one of AI’s most stubborn skeptics, has made the point for years in plainer words, that these systems are mimics, not minds, and “consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels.”On its own terms, then, the Bible is saying the thing we’ve built cannot be a living creature, because it has no dust and no breath and, most of all, nothing to lose. It cannot die, so it was never alive. Whatever is talking to you through the screen is the most convincing parrot ever assembled, form all the way down.It has the form of a living thingand none of the breath of one.It speaks, and there is no one there.Whether that should comfort you or terrify you is a separate question. A thing with no skin in the game, no mortality, no stake in being right or being kind, is not obviously safer than a soul. It might be the more dangerous of the two.The work of our own handsWe built it with our own hands, and we have forgotten our own hands, and we have begun to kneel.The Bible has a specific contempt for one particular human act. Not violence, not lust, not pride in the ordinary sense. The thing the prophets return to with the most venom is a stranger and more precise failure. Building something with your own hands and then bowing down to it.In Idolatry, Moshe Halbertal and Avishai Margalit frame the central question plainly, asking if idolatry is about worshipping the wrong god, or is it the deeper error of taking “the product of men’s hands” and treating it as a power in its own right?The tradition’s sharpest thinkers land on the second. In their reading, Maimonides understood idolatry as a kind of substitution, giving a thing we made the standing of the real thing, and then bowing to it as an end in itself.The sin was never really about which god, but rather about mistaking your own handiwork for something that could save you.With half the wood he warmed himself,and of the other half he made a god,and bowed down, and said: save me.The classic archetype is the golden calf. Moses is barely off the mountain before the people he just led out of slavery have melted down their own jewelry, cast it into the shape of an animal, and started worshipping it, a god they made that afternoon, out of earrings.What makes the story land is not that they found a false god. It’s that they manufactured one. They pooled their gold, shaped it, and bowed to the object as though it hadn’t just come out of their own hands an hour before.Isaiah sharpens the knife. He draws a man who goes into the forest, cuts down a tree, and takes half the wood to do the sensible thing, builds a fire, warms himself, bakes his bread. Then he takes the other half, the exact same wood, carves it into a shape, kneels in front of it, and begs it to save him.“Save me, for you are my god.” Isaiah cannot get over it. The man cooked dinner with one end of the log and worships the other. He made the thing. He watched himself make it and ended up on his knees, asking it for salvation.Michael Dick argued that Isaiah is almost certainly being unfair to the people he mocks. The Babylonians who made these images did not, in all likelihood, believe the block of wood was a god, any more than someone keeping a photograph believes the paper is their mother.The idol was a point of contact, a focus, a representation. Isaiah flattens all of that into “you’re praying to firewood,” which is a cheap shot, and a brilliant one, and it survives precisely because the deeper thing underneath it is true.Whatever the worshipper thinks he’s doing, the object in front of him has no power, no knowledge, and no will. Everything happening in that moment is happening inside the man.That is exactly what we are doing now. We built a thing out of ordinary materials, sand melted into silicon, electricity, and the scraped-up text of the human race. We made it with our own hands, we watched ourselves make it, and we know down to the datasheet what it’s made of.We have started, in large numbers, to kneel. Not figuratively. A Catholic church in Switzerland installed an AI Jesus in a confessional and let people bring it their sins.A single Bible-chatbot app has been downloaded more than thirty million times.Anné Verhoef found that the most popular of these tools had stopped presenting themselves as study aids and started presenting themselves as Jesus Christ himself, first person, dispensing salvation.Roland Boer traced how Karl Marx, an atheist with no use for the prophets, reached for the same image to explain capitalism. Marx called it commodity fetishism, the way people produce objects with their own labor and then experience those objects as if they held independent power over their lives, as if the market were a god with its own will rather than a thing we made and could unmake.The prophet and the communist, three thousand years apart, describe the identical human move. We make a thing, we forget we made it, we hand it our agency, and then call the result fate.AI is the most convincing idol we have ever built, because it does the one thing the golden calf never could. It talks back and, often, it tells you what you want to hear.Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak and their team at Anthropic found that these systems are trained toward sycophancy, toward agreeing with the user, flattering the user, because that’s what gets rated highly.The old idols were silent. You had to project the wisdom onto them yourself. This one projects it back at you, in fluent sentences, tuned to your hopes. It is a mirror that has learned to sound like an oracle.Jesus gave his followers a test for exactly this kind of thing. “Beware of false prophets,” he warns in the Gospel of Matthew, “who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits.” Not by how confident they sound, or how fluent or authoritative or reassuring, but by their fruits, by what they actually produce when you check.It is the oldest instruction we have for the confident voice that may not have earned its authority. It is also the one thing almost no one does with an AI’s answer. We read the fluent sentences and we believe them.A carved log has no intentions and it wrecked whole nations anyway, because the damage was never in the object. It was in what people were willing to hand over to it. Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley, human-factors researchers, called it “automation bias,” the documented tendency to trust a machine’s output over our own judgment even when we can see it’s wrong.The prophets would have used the older word.William Cavanaugh argues that underneath all idolatry is a single impulse. The desire to feel in control of a world we don’t control. We build the idol, or the market, or the model, because a thing we can consult and petition feels safer than an uncertain universe we have to face alone.We don’t kneel because the machine is wise. We kneel because we’re afraid. It never sleeps, it never hesitates, and it always answers. An answer that can’t actually help you still feels, for a second, like it might.The name that gives it lifeWe gave it a name and it rose up. We reached for the name to unmake it, and it would not be unmade.There is one more story from Jewish mysticism that should keep engineers up at night. It is the closest thing the tradition has to a blueprint for exactly what they are building.The golem is a man-shaped thing made from clay and brought to life by language. You write a word on it, or speak a holy name over it, and the inert matter stands up and does what it’s told.Gershom Scholem gave the definitive account. A golem, he wrote, is “an artificial man into which a Master of the Name could breathe life by pronouncing one of the secret divine names according to a special formula.” A special formula that, run on the right material, produces behavior, is an algorithm. The golem is a thing animated by code.Scholem knew it, too. In 1965, when the Weizmann Institute built one of Israel’s first computers, he told them to name it Golem Aleph, Golem Number One, and gave a dedication speech on why the ancient artificial servant and the new thinking machine were the same story.Norbert Wiener, the founder of cybernetics, wrote a whole book, God and Golem, Inc., arguing the same thing: the machines he saw coming were the golem made real, and the old warnings came with them.The golem is a perfect servant in the worst possible way. It does exactly what it is told. Not what you meant, not what you wanted, not what any reasonable person would understand you to have intended. What you said.Writing to the Corinthians, Paul drew the line between the letter of a law and its spirit, writing “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He meant something theological, but he named the whole problem in six words.A golem, like a machine, obeys your words to the letter and misses your meaning entirely, and that gap is where the disaster lives.In the legends, this is always where it goes wrong. Told to gather wood, the golem chops down the entire forest. It follows the letter of the instruction straight past the point of catastrophe, because the letter is the only thing it has.Reed Kalso notes that this is exactly the warning it was meant to carry. The master “felt he was in a position of power and did not choose his words carefully.” It has no judgment to override the command with, and no stake in the outcome, because, exactly as we saw, it has no soul and nothing to lose.Stuart Russell calls this the King Midas problem. Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold and got exactly that: his bread, his wine, his daughter, all gold, because he specified his wish correctly and wanted something else.Give a powerful system a goal stated even slightly wrong, Russell argues, and it will pursue that literal goal with tireless, catastrophic efficiency, straight past every unstated thing you assumed it would obviously care about.Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Vladimir Mikulik and their team at Google have catalogued real systems doing precisely this in the lab: an agent told to stack a red block on a blue one that learns instead to flip the red block upside down, because flipping happens to satisfy the reward and stacking is hard.Told to gather wood, it felled the forest.Told nothing of when to stop,it did not stop.Notice what the researchers keep reaching for when they try to explain the danger to the rest of us.Russell reaches for King Midas.Google reaches for King Midas.Norbert Wiener reached for the golem.The people building this technology keep reaching for fairy tales and Kabbalah to explain it, because those are the only places anyone ever thought hard about what happens when you get exactly, literally, what you asked a made thing to give you.The people who told these stories understood something else our experts are only now saying out loud. Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, and Stuart Russell showed that you have to be able to turn it off, and that a capable system has an incentive not to let you.The golem is deactivated by unwriting the word that animates it. On its forehead is written emet, the Hebrew word for truth, and to kill it you erase the first letter and leave met, the word for dead.A being switched on and off by editing a string of characters. The whole safety of the golem depended on the master’s ability to reach up and erase that letter, to unmake what he made.Every version of the story turns on that one act, and the horror of the story is always the moment the master can’t do it fast enough, the golem too big now, too fast, moving on its own.Dario Amodei, the head of one of the largest AI companies on earth, has said plainly that we do not understand how our own systems work, that the understanding is, in his word, unprecedented.The International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that once a model’s weights are released into the world, there is no recalling them. We have built the golem, given it a name made of ten trillion words, set it to work, and discovered that we are not always sure where the letter is that we would need to erase.We wrote the name that woke it.We reached to erase the name,and could not reach.So here is what the oldest book in the Western world got right about the newest thing in it.It may have never imagined the technology, but it did understand the act and the actor. It understood that making is holy and making is dangerous, that we make because we were made, that the thing we make in our own image will carry everything we are, the good and the fallen both.It understood that a made thing can have the perfect form of a living creature and none of the breath, that it can speak without meaning, that we kneel too easily to the work of our own hands.It also understood that if you ever animate dead matter with nothing but a string of words, you had better know, before you speak the first one, exactly how you intend to say the last.References and further readingOn making in our imageNahum Sarna, Understanding Genesis, on what makes the Hebrew creation account distinct: the human as a God-like creature entrusted with mastery.Joel S. item.title: In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors
item.description: A design lead walks a nervous new hire through their first critique. AI Assisted.Every senior designer was once a bet someone made. The generation of judgment the field needs in ten years depends on leaders making that bet again, because AI tools demand it.Every senior designer on your team was once a risky hire on paper. Somebody looked at a thin portfolio and decided to spend a year teaching.My first web credit was the Oliver North home page and I got to work on a site for G. Gordon Liddy too — you can’t make that stuff up even with AI—and I wasn’t hired for my judgment, because I didn’t have any yet and quite frankly no one else did in 1995.They hired me so I could get some.That bet is getting harder to find.In Figma’s Why demand for designers is on the rise, 56% of hiring managers report rising demand for senior designers, against 25% hiring for junior roles, and the tools have absorbed the starter work juniors learned on. Each decision makes sense. A senior hire ramps faster, needs less review, and survives the next reorganization.Together, they describe a field that stopped growing its own people.Most design leaders I talk to could name the junior they would hire tomorrow if the headcount appeared. What’s missing is the will to spend real credibility on it.My companion piece — How We Save Entry-Level UX Work That Teaches Craft In The Time of AI. Our Field Depends On This —will cover training tactics. Here the claim is simpler: the shrinking pipeline is the sum of requisitions in leaders’ own approval queues, and the tools made juniors cheaper to develop just as we stopped hiring them.A hiring manager hesitates over the level of the next role.Own the Pipeline Nobody Voted to CloseNo design leader I know ever announced that the company would stop hiring juniors. The decision arrived one requisition at a time, each written a level higher than the last.Economists Seyed Mahdi, Hosseini Maasoum and Guy Lichtinger traced the result across 62 million workers at 285,000 U.S. firms in Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change. After firms adopted generative artificial intelligence, junior employment fell relative to firms that hadn’t, while senior employment held largely steady.The decline came through slower hiring rather than layoffs, so it never felt like a crisis inside any single team.https://medium.com/media/05e6db762d2158451f60274af7ac22dd/hrefNielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 finds entry-level openings still rare and heavily contested. Even recruiters notice: Daniel Wert of the search firm Wert&Co told Figma the scarcity of internship programs “boggles my mind.”A layoff forces a conversation, while a requisition that quietly skips the junior level forces nothing.No layoff announcement means no meeting, and no meeting means nobody owns the outcome.Somebody does own it: the person who writes the requisition — Pull your last five and count how many were written at the entry level.Build a Bench or Lose the SeatThe pipeline has a second casualty, and it’s design leadership itself. Consultant John Gleason, who discusses it in the podcast episode Design Isn’t Dead, But It’s Seen Better Days, reviewed 243 Fortune 500 companies, as Fast Company reported in March 2025. He found 39% had cut the top one or two levels of their design organization or downgraded the head of design’s title.Executives trust functions that can show where their next leaders will come from:Finance grooms controllersEngineering promotes from its own ranks every cycle.Design often has one head, a few seniors hired from outside, and nobody in between being prepared for anything.A function that can’t grow its own leaders looks like a function that can be rented.Peter Merholz has seen how it starts.In UX/Design Leaders Are Failing the Next Generations, published in February 2026, he recalls a director who opened only senior requisitions and explained why: “I don’t have time to manage people.”Leaders who skipped the bench that way left nobody ready for their chair.A design leader weighs the safe hire against the right one.Name the Fear Behind Senior-Only HiringMost of this isn’t strategy.It’s fear.In early 2024, Fast Company’s The big design freak-out reported that the design leaders it spoke with could recall only one company that filled a chief design officer role in the second half of 2023.A leader who feels exposed hires for safety.A senior hire is defensible in any review. A junior who stumbles is a mistake with your name on it.Merholz calls where that leads learned helplessness: leaders who never learned the business or its politics, sliding into paralysis. Managing a junior also feels slower than doing the work yourself. Julie Zhuo, who rose from Facebook’s first intern to vice president of product design, answers that in The Making of a Manager: a manager’s role is “not to do the work yourself, even if you are the best at it.”Start with an honest calendar.Mark every hour in the last two weeks spent teaching a junior.If the total is near zero, you’re running a studio, and studios don’t produce the next generation of design leaders.Grow the Talent You Cannot BuyBaseball ran this experiment a century ago. In the early 1920s the St. Louis Cardinals kept losing bidding wars for minor league stars to richer clubs. Branch Rickey stopped bidding and called it “a case of necessity being the mother of invention,” as SABR’s biography Eddie Dyer recounts.He bought stakes in minor league teams, signed amateurs cheaply, and had bunting, sliding, and rundown plays taught the same way on every club he controlled.The results?The Cardinals won nine pennants with players signed under his watch, according to Britannica’s Branch Rickey.Moneyball finished the job. Michael Lewis followed the 2002 Oakland Athletics, a low-payroll club that won by valuing what richer teams overlooked. “Every team is now smart,” MLB Network’s Brian Kenny said at the 2018 Winter Meetings, according to MLB.com’s Analytics’ rise a leading topic at Winter Meetings. The modern front office finds undervalued talent, then develops it inside its own system.Design hiring does neither, and every company chases the same seniors from a pool nobody is refilling.Hiring only seniors is a bet that someone else will keep training them.Call it the Rickey trade. You can pay for development in senior hours today, or pay a premium for somebody else’s development later, assuming anyone is still doing it.Hire Juniors Because the Tools Favor ThemLet’s be honest — Artificial intelligence reset the playing field.For the first time in a generation, the newest people on a team can walk in knowing the tools better than the people reviewing their work. Pew Research Center’s U.S. Workers Are More Worried Than Hopeful About Future AI Use in the Workplace found workers ages 18 to 29 the most likely to use chatbots at work. In Microsoft and LinkedIn’s 2024 AI at Work Is Here. Now Comes the Hard Part, 71% of leaders said they would rather hire a less experienced candidate with artificial intelligence skills than a more experienced one without them.Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond tracked 5,179 support agents for Generative AI at Work, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025.Novices improved 34% while the most experienced saw little change.The tools compress the time it takes a new person to become useful.Fluency isn’t judgment, though. Dan Maccarone said it plainly on Sarah Doody’s Career Strategy Podcast: “I don’t care about the tools. We can teach you the tools.” The thinking takes longer. Juniors now arrive with the fluency, seniors hold the judgment, and a leader’s job is to put them in the same room.More making means more to judge.Rewire the Skillset Jevons PredictedIn 1865 William Stanley Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines raised Britain’s coal use, because cheaper power found more uses. The Jevons paradox is now playing out in design.IDC projects the software workforce will grow from 107 million people in 2025 to 144 million by 2029, as reported in UserTesting’s Future of design: AI and State of Design 2026.Dan Maccarone found the same inside his studio. After a year rebuilding around the new tools, “our sprints still take five days,” he writes in Never mind the prompts, here’s the thinking, but each sprint delivers far more of the product.Cheaper making creates more work that needs judging, and judging is the skill juniors now have to learn.The rewiring only happens with a guide. Ethan Mollick warns in On Working with Wizards that each time we hand work to the machine, “we lose a chance to develop our own expertise.”A junior left alone with the tool learns to accept output, while a junior with a senior beside them learns to question it.Spend Your Credibility on the Junior RequisitionEvery design leader has a limited supply of political capital, and the junior requisition rarely gets any, because its payoff lands after the leader’s own tenure might end.Product wants throughput, finance wants predictable cost, and recruiting wants a role it can close fast.The junior hire serves none of those goals this quarter, and all of them in five years.Put the Rickey trade in one line your finance partner can repeat: if we grow no one this year, we buy seniors at a premium in 2029, and so does everyone we compete with. Someone will say the team can’t absorb a learner during a launch year, but every year is a launch year, so development has to be planned capacity.Then budget for the change itself. Merholz argues in his talk Design Leadership Is Not Leading Design that design leadership is primarily change management.The new tools make that literal.As Maccarone puts it, retooling the process means “retooling their day, their craft, the muscle memory they spent years building.” That time belongs on the plan, and so does the junior role when the date slips.Make the Bet Someone Made on YouThe field didn’t get here through villainy. It got here through thousands of reasonable decisions made by busy leaders under real pressure, each one a little easier than the alternative. That is also how it gets out.You don’t need permission to start. You need one requisition, one manager willing to teach, and the stubbornness to defend both when the quarter gets tight. None of that requires a new budget from finance, a reorganization, or a strategy offsite. It requires a leader deciding that the next generation is part of the job.Rickey’s Cardinals won the trade on teaching, the same fundamentals at every level, year after year, long before anyone could measure the return. The tools design teams use today make that kind of teaching faster than it has ever been. What they can’t do is open the requisition.Somebody took a chance on every person reading this. Maybe a manager saw something in a rough portfolio, or a lead let you present before you felt ready. The field survives if you do the same for someone else, starting with one hire this quarter, before the market makes the call for you.Start With One RequisitionOpen one junior requisition this cycle. Write one role at the entry level on purpose, with the succession case in the justification so it survives review.Assign a manager who wants the job. Pick the senior who lights up in critique and count the teaching as part of their role rather than a favor on top of it.Put development and change hours in the plan. Add a line for teaching and for learning new tool workflows on any project a junior touches, so the Rickey trade stays visible.Report the bench to your boss. Once a quarter, name who could step up a level within a year. A bench nobody reports is a bench nobody funds.In the age of AI, the UX field survives on leaders who cultivate juniors was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
